body.x: Search online for the nikah khutba and you will find dozens of pages, each presenting a slightly different Arabic text as if it were the standard one. If your own wedding is approaching, that can be quietly unsettling: which version will be read at your ceremony, and what will it actually say? The honest answer is that there is no single fixed script — and that is not a gap in the tradition. The khutba has a recognisable shape, a classic set of Quranic verses, and a purpose every couple can understand before the day. This guide explains its structure, the verses you are most likely to hear and what they mean, who delivers the khutba, and what to listen for when it is recited over your own marriage.
First, an honest answer about 'the' text

In Shia practice, the sermon before the contract is a recommended and beloved part of the ceremony, but the legal heart of the nikah is the contract itself — the offer and acceptance (the sigha) spoken in Arabic, usually through representatives (wakeels) acting for the bride and groom. The khutba frames that contract; it does not replace it. Because the sermon is not a fixed legal formula, its wording is chosen by the reciter. One scholar may keep it short and almost entirely Quranic; another may add passages of counsel; a family with a long tradition may ask for the version an elder recited at weddings for forty years. Any 'full text and translation' you find online is therefore one reciter's khutba, faithfully written down — a good guide to the genre, but not an official script your officiant has failed to follow if his differs from it.
The shape of the khutba, part by part
For all that variation, the architecture is remarkably consistent across Shia ceremonies, from Hyderabad to London to Toronto. A typical khutba moves through the same stations, in roughly this order:

Praise of Allah (hamd) — the reciter opens by glorifying God, often with words drawn from the opening of the Quran itself
Salawat — blessings on the Prophet Muhammad and on his family, the Ahl al-Bayt, woven through the sermon rather than confined to one place
Quranic verses — a small, classic set of passages about creation, marriage and God-consciousness, discussed below
Counsel — a short exhortation to the couple and the witnesses about the weight of the covenant being entered
Dua for the couple — the reciter asks Allah to bless this specific marriage, usually naming the bride and groom
The contract — the khutba ends and the sigha itself begins: the offer, the acceptance, and the mahr stated aloud

Notice what the structure is doing. It begins with God, moves to gratitude and blessing, grounds the marriage in scripture, speaks honestly about responsibility, and only then turns to the legal act. The couple are not rushed to the signature. They are first reminded — in front of everyone who loves them — of what kind of act this is. Many couples say afterwards that the khutba was the moment the day stopped feeling like an event and started feeling like a covenant. That is exactly what it is designed to do.
The verses you will almost certainly hear

Three themes recur so reliably that you can prepare for them. The first is creation: the opening of Surah al-Nisa (4:1), which speaks of humanity created from a single soul, and from it its mate, and which joins God-consciousness to the ties of kinship — asking, in effect, that the new bond be held with the same reverence owed to God and to family. It is chosen because it places marriage inside the story of creation itself, and because it names kinship: two families are being woven together, not just two people.

The second is the verse couples remember most, from Surah al-Rum (30:21): that God created spouses so that hearts may find tranquillity in one another, and that He placed love (mawadda) and mercy (rahma) between them. Reciters linger on those two words — affection for the days of ease, mercy for the days when affection is hard. The third theme is taqwa, God-consciousness, often through verses recited in sermons for centuries (such as 3:102 and 33:70–71), which urge the believers to be mindful of Allah and to speak words that are straight and true. Some reciters add the beautiful image from Surah al-Baqarah (2:187) of spouses as garments for one another — covering, protecting and adorning. The wording around the verses varies; the verses themselves are the stable core, and you can read them in any reliable translation before the day.
Who delivers it, and when in the ceremony

The khutba is usually delivered by the officiating scholar — the aalim who will oversee the contract — though in some families a respected elder or the bride's representative recites it. It comes at the start of the ceremony proper: guests are seated, the groom and witnesses are present, and in many traditions the bride listens from an adjoining room with her wakeel beside her, her consent carried into the room by him. In diaspora ceremonies it is now common for the reciter to pause and explain the sermon's meaning in English, Urdu or the community's language — a small kindness that changes the room, because guests who understand the words stop treating the khutba as a prelude and start treating it as the point. If that matters to you, ask your officiant about it in advance; most are glad to be asked.
What to listen for on the day

You will be nervous, and much of it will wash over you — that is normal, and nobody is testing you. But three moments are worth catching. First, the turn from praise to counsel, when the reciter addresses the couple directly: this is the tradition speaking to you personally. Second, the dua made for you by name, when the whole room says amin over your marriage — many couples remember that sound for the rest of their lives. Third, the contract that follows: listen for your names spoken correctly, and for the mahr stated clearly and without embarrassment. If you can, ask the officiant beforehand for the order of service, or even a copy of the khutba he intends to recite. Read it once, quietly, the week before. On the day itself, you will hear it not as a stranger, but as someone who knows where they are in the story.

excerpt: There is no single fixed khutba text, but there is a recognisable shape, a classic set of verses, and a meaning worth understanding before your own wedding day.
title: Shia Nikah Khutba: The Text, Its Structure and What It Means
